articles.title: Colombia’s far-right president faces first round of major protests
articles.author: BreakThrough News
articles.content_excerpt: On October 14, tens of thousands of Colombians took to the streets to protest against the government of far-right leader Abelardo de la Espriella, who has been in office for just two months. The protests demonstrated the opposition’s clear ability to mobilize its base and fill the streets of several Colombian cities, even though the new government is still in its early days. Protesters – including members of labor unions, Indigenous organizations, opposition parties, and students – marched through the streets of the capital, Bogotá, as well as other major cities across the country, such as Cali, Medellín, Bucaramanga, Riohacha, and Pereira. articles.title: Nobel Peace Laureate Navi Pillay on ICC, Gaza, Rape as War Crime, Her South African Roots & Mandela
articles.content_excerpt: We speak with the acclaimed South African human rights lawyer and international jurist Navi Pillay, who was awarded this year’s Nobel Peace Prize. Pillay has been the United Nations high commissioner for human rights and a judge at both the International Criminal Court and at an international tribunal investigating the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. Most recently, she led the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. articles.title: A Wealth Tax on Billionaires? California Voters to Decide Prop 40
articles.content_excerpt: As voters across the United States cast ballots on November 3, Californians are weighing whether to approve a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires in the state. The tax would apply to roughly 250 Californians who now hold an estimated $2.3 trillion in wealth. Supporters say the wealth tax could raise up to $100 billion, with about 90% going toward healthcare. The remaining funds would support education and food assistance programs. If Proposition 40 passes, it will mark the first time a government in the U.S. successfully taxes the wealth — rather than just the income — of the ultra-rich. “It’s past time that billionaires pay their fair share,” says Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, which is backing the initiative. articles.title: ‘Nuke Brazil’ Missile Prop Exposes Cozy Bolsonaro-Trump relationship
articles.content_excerpt: On Sunday, October 18, supporters of presidential candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro paraded down Paulista Avenue in São Paulo, clutching an inflatable toy missile bearing a call for a nuclear strike on Brazil. Senator Bolsonaro, who attended the rally with allies such as far right Rep. Nikolas Ferreira, made no comment about it. The white structure, raised above the crowd, bore the English language inscription “Trump nuke Brazil.” Images from the event show people dressed in green and yellow standing near the object, draped in Brazilian flags. By calling on a foreign power to launch a nuclear attack on their own country, these demonstrators took a stance that amounts to treason and a direct affront to Brazilian sovereignty. articles.title: Burkina Faso: Thomas Sankara, the cut-short revolution, and the legacy of feminism
articles.author: Editor
articles.content_excerpt: The original distinctiveness of Sankarist thought lies in having simultaneously attacked three pillars of structural oppression: imperialist dependence, through the outright rejection of international public debt, defined as a “neocolonial instrument of reconquest and the economic assassination of peoples”; the internal class structure and bureaucratic rent, through the dismantling of the privileges of the parasitic state bourgeoisie—nourished by French aid funds and disconnected from the material needs of the peasant masses; and patriarchal oppression. articles.title: Food aid cut for half a million Palestinians in Gaza, as fatal Israeli strikes continue
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content_excerpt: At least eight Palestinians, including four children, were killed in Israeli assaults in different parts of the Gaza Strip over the last two days. On Monday, October 19, Israeli forces launched drone strikes on north-central Gaza City and the southern city of Khan Younis, killing a Palestinian man and two children. One day earlier, five Palestinians were killed and several others were injured in Israeli shelling and gunfire across the besieged enclave. This includes two children, who were shot dead by Israeli soldiers in separate attacks. One of the slain children was identified as 13-year-old Tamer Soboh , who was killed in the northern city of Beit Lahia; the other was Misk al-Dalu , who died after Israeli troops opened fire at tents sheltering displaced people in al-Maghazi refugee camp

articles.title: Curfews imposed in French cities as rebellion against austerity grows nationwide
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content_excerpt: Mass mobilizations against austerity policies and their effects are not winding down in France. On Saturday, October 17 , roughly 800,000 people joined protests across more than 1,700 assembly points, according to union figures – amplifying demands tabled over a month of student protests and demanding urgent action on the cost of living crisis. In the aftermath of the protests, the government expanded local authorities’ powers to introduce curfews. This led to overnight movement limitation orders introduced in several cities, including central parts of Paris, Lille, Lyon, and Nice. Many of the curfews target young people in particular, reflecting institutional concern about the success of their recent mobilizations. articles.title: Students across the US South demand justice for Nolan Wells
articles.author: Devin B. Martinez
articles.content_excerpt: Calls for justice and for the reopening of Nolan Wells’ case are mounting after a grand jury declined to bring criminal charges, despite the question of Wells’ cause of death remaining unanswered. Wells, a young Black student at Southwest Mississippi Community College, went on a boating trip on July 4 to Horn Island, just off the coast of Mississippi, with several white friends. He never returned. His friends, who returned to the mainland with Wells’ cell phone but without him, claimed he chose to stay behind.
